items.title: What the passe compose replaced
items.claim: In modern spoken French, the passe compose has largely replaced which other tense?
items.reveal_title: Passe simple has retreated to formal writing
items.reveal:
Spoken French uses the passe compose where 19th-century literature used the passe simple. The simple form survives in formal narrative writing, historical writing, and some regional usage.

The shift has been described in detail by linguists since at least Damourette and Pichon (1911-1936).
items.why: Grammatical structures can fall out of speech but persist in writing for generations.

items.title: Languages spoken in France in 1789
items.claim: Abbe Gregoire's 1794 report estimated what proportion of French citizens spoke standard French as a native language at the time of the Revolution?
items.reveal_title: A small minority spoke standard French
items.reveal:
Gregoire's report 'Rapport sur la necessite et les moyens d'aneantir les patois' estimated that only around 3 million of 25 million inhabitants spoke French well; many used Occitan, Breton, Alsatian, Basque or other languages.

Universal primary education in the late 19th century did much of the standardisation.
items.why: Modern national languages are often the product of policy as much as organic spread.

items.title: Where most French speakers will live
items.claim: OIF (Observatoire de la langue francaise) projections suggest that by 2050, roughly what share of French speakers will live in Africa?
items.reveal_title: Most French speakers will be African
items.reveal:
OIF estimates (Demographie et langue francaise reports) project that demographic growth in francophone Africa will lift the African share of French speakers to around 85% by 2050.

This follows from population growth in countries such as DR Congo, where French is an official or working language.
items.why: The geographic centre of a language can shift dramatically across a generation.
